meta.task: Split the orders table into orders and order_items and move production onto the new schema without downtime or data loss
meta.title: Migrate a Production Schema Safely
meta.promptIntro: Split the orders table into orders and order_items and move production onto the new schema without downtime or data loss. Plan it outward from the callers: a rehearsed migration, a verified backfill, a cutover the team signs off on, and a rollback path that stays open until the old shape is finally dropped.

nodes.label: Gather the schema, the traffic, and the rules
nodes.description: Collect the current schema and row counts, the peak-traffic windows, how much downtime is acceptable, and what rollback has to look like if the cutover goes wrong.

nodes.label: Grep every repo for the table name
nodes.description: Search the monolith and every service for the string 'orders' and wade through the hits, one repo at a time.

nodes.label: Chase the ORM models and raw SQL
nodes.description: Follow the models, scopes, and hand-written SQL in background jobs to find which code actually reads and writes the columns.

nodes.label: Hunt the callers nobody owns
nodes.description: Track down the analytics queries, cron scripts, and one-off jobs that touch the table outside the app — the caller you miss is the outage.

nodes.label: Design the target schema
nodes.description: Decide the new tables, keys, indexes and constraints, and exactly how every row of the old shape maps onto them.

nodes.label: Write forward and rollback migrations
nodes.description: Write the DDL both ways, in steps small enough that neither direction holds a lock for long.

nodes.label: Dry-run on a production-sized copy
nodes.description: Restore a recent dump, run the migration against it, time every statement, and watch what takes locks and for how long.

nodes.label: Lock window acceptable?
nodes.description: Does the slowest statement fit inside the window the team agreed to, on production-sized data?

nodes.label: Write and babysit the backfill
nodes.description: Move millions of rows in resumable chunks, throttled so replication does not fall behind, checked on for hours and restarted wherever it stalls.

nodes.label: Ship dual-write and compare the shapes
nodes.description: Write to both schemas at once, then compare counts and checksums to find the rows where the two disagree.

nodes.label: Parity clean?
nodes.description: Do old and new agree on every row, or is there drift to chase back into the backfill?

nodes.label: Cutover go/no-go with the team
nodes.description: Walk the plan, the rollback and the window with whoever has to be awake for it, and get the go.

nodes.label: Run the cutover in the window
nodes.description: Work the checklist at midnight: pause writes, run the switch, point the app at the new shape, with everyone watching a dashboard.

nodes.label: Reads correct in production?
nodes.description: Are queries returning the right rows at the right latency, or is something quietly wrong on the new shape?

nodes.label: Drop the old shape once it is quiet
nodes.description: After a safe interval with nothing reading the old columns, drop them and reclaim the space.

nodes.label: Schema migrated
nodes.description: Production runs on the new schema, the backfill is verified, and the rollback path is documented for as long as it was needed.

suggestions.name: DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp
suggestions.claim: Sub-millisecond architectural queries over a whole codebase — up to 99% fewer tokens.
suggestions.promptFragment: Before you design anything, ask DeusData/codebase-memory-mcp who reads and writes the orders table, instead of grepping the monolith and every service for its name and chasing the ORM models, jobs, and one-off scripts by hand. Query it for the models, queries and jobs that touch those columns and treat that answer as the migration's blast radius.

replaceWith.label: Query the graph for every caller
replaceWith.description: One structural query returns the readers and writers of the table — the models, the jobs, and the scripts a grep for the table name would miss.
